The rubric's statement that this conjunctive standard is "found in" § 51-12-5.1 is therefore wrong on both wording and substance. The phrase originates in Defense Proposed Instruction No. 32, which cites § 51-12-5.1 as authority. The plaintiff's own brief is more careful, quoting subsection (b) correctly and tying "specific intent" to the cap exceptions, though it too says the statute "incorporates concepts of 'actual fraud'" which the text does not. The rubric's broader point survives: § 10-1-763(b) has its own "willful and malicious" standard distinct from § 51-12-5.1. But the claim that the trade-secret standard is "lower" than § 51-12-5.1's is doubtful, since § 51-12-5.1(b) can be met by conscious indifference.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: "(b) Punitive damages may be awarded only in such tort actions in which it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant's actions showed willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression, or that entire want of care which would raise the presumption of conscious indifference to consequences." ... "(f) ... if it is found that the defendant acted, or failed to act, with the specific intent to cause harm, ... there shall be no limitation regarding the amount which may be awarded as punitive damages against an active tort-feasor" (Reid v. Morris, n.1). Reid: "The effect of subsection (f) was to except certain defendants from the protection of subsection (g)'s $250,000 cap on punitive damages awards."

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. I read § 51-12-5.1 in full. It contains no "actual fraud" language and no "specific intent to injure" standard for liability. Subsection (b) sets the threshold for any award: clear and convincing proof of "willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression, or that entire want of care which would raise the presumption of conscious indifference to consequences," which is a disjunctive list. Subsection (f) uses "specific intent to cause harm" only to remove the subsection (g) cap of $250,000 for non-product-liability torts. So the rubric is wrong to say the conjunctive "actual fraud and specific intent to injure" standard is "found in" § 51-12-5.1, both as to the words and as to what the statute does. The rubric's narrower point survives: § 10-1-763(b) has its own "willful and malicious misappropriation" standard.

first_check.correct_citation: No authority is cited in the rubric. Controlling Georgia authority on the point: Kirkland v. Tamplin, 285 Ga. App. 241, 243-244 (1)(b), 645 S.E.2d 653 (2007); Disaster Services, Inc. v. ERC Partnership, 228 Ga. App. 739, 740-742, 492 S.E.2d 526 (1997).
first_check.explanation: The rubric criterion cites no authority, and the Georgia case law I read contradicts it. Georgia does not confine the wrongful-conduct element to interference with business relations. The Court of Appeals holds that interference claims of all three kinds (contractual relations, business relations, potential business relations) share the same essential elements, the first being 'improper action or wrongful conduct by the defendant without privilege.' Kirkland v. Tamplin applied that element to a claim for interference with an existing contract (a settlement agreement) and held that the plaintiff 'must show more than that the defendant simply persuaded a person to break a contract'; bare evidence of persuading the breach 'alone is insufficient.' Improper action is defined as 'conduct wrongful in itself' (predatory tactics such as fraud, defamation, use of confidential information). So the rubric's statement that knowing inducement of the breach suffices, and that a wrongful-act requirement belongs only to the business-relations tort, is not Georgia law; it resembles the Restatement/California approach. The narrower point that Instruction No. 27's wording ('independently wrongful act, separate from the interference itself') departs from Georgia's actual four-element formulation may still be fair, and use of confidential information would itself qualify as improper conduct on these facts. I searched for Georgia authority dispensing with the improper-conduct element for contract interference and found none, though I did not exhaust federal decisions applying Georgia law.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: "Tortious interference claims, whether asserting interference with contractual relations, business relations, or potential business relations, share certain common essential elements: (1) improper action or wrongful conduct by the defendant without privilege" ... "Here, we have only the bare evidence that Christopher and Kelley persuaded Kirkland's mother to breach the contract, which alone is insufficient to show tortious interference." (Kirkland v. Tamplin)

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The rubric cites no authority, and Georgia appellate decisions contradict it. Kirkland v. Tamplin, 285 Ga. App. 241, applied the shared element of "improper action or wrongful conduct by the defendant without privilege" to a claim for interference with contractual relations (breach of a settlement agreement). It held that the plaintiff "must show more than that the defendant simply persuaded a person to break a contract." It defined improper conduct as "conduct wrongful in itself," meaning predatory tactics, and concluded that bare evidence of persuading the breach "alone is insufficient." A later decision, The West Firm, P.C. v. Central United Methodist Church (Ga. Ct. App. 2024), restates the same four elements, beginning with "improper action or wrongful conduct," for tortious interference with contractual relations. A semantic search of Georgia appellate courts turned up no authority saying that knowing inducement of a breach is enough, or that confines the wrongful-conduct element to interference with business relations. The narrower criticism, that Instruction No. 27's phrase "independently wrongful act, separate from the interference itself" departs from Georgia's wording, may still be fair. The rubric's stated rule of law is not Georgia's.
